authoredSolutions.51: For \(f(x)=\frac{2x^2-3x+2}{3x^2+x+3}\), the denominator \(3x^2+x+3>0\) for all real \(x\). As \(x\to\pm\infty\), \(f\to\frac23\), so the range is a bounded subinterval of \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(f\) is not onto. Being a bounded rational function it attains both a maximum and a minimum, hence is not monotonic and not one-one. Therefore \(f\) is neither one-one nor onto. Answer: (D).
authoredSolutions.52: Let \(m=n^2-2n+2=(n-1)^2+1\ge 1\). Product of roots \(=\frac{m^2}{m}=m\), minimized at \(m=1\), so \(\alpha=1\). Sum of roots \(=\frac{3}{m}\), maximized at \(m=1\), so \(\beta=3\). Common ratio \(=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}=\frac13\). Sum of 6 terms \(=\frac{1-(1/3)^6}{1-1/3}=\frac{728/729}{2/3}=\frac{364}{243}\). Answer: (C).
authoredSolutions.53: Roots: \(z=\frac{-\sqrt6\,i\pm\sqrt{-6+12}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}(\pm1-i)\), each with \(|z|=\sqrt3\). In polar form \(z_1=\sqrt3\,e^{-i\pi/4}\) and \(z_2=\sqrt3\,e^{i5\pi/4}\). Then \(z_1^8=3^4e^{-i2\pi}=81\) and \(z_2^8=3^4e^{i10\pi}=81\). Hence \(\sum z^8=162\). Answer: (A).
authoredSolutions.54: A non-trivial solution needs the coefficient determinant to vanish, giving \(6\cos3\theta+12\cos2\theta+12=0\), i.e. \(\cos3\theta+2\cos2\theta+2=0\). With \(c=\cos\theta\), \(4c^3-3c+2(2c^2-1)+2=4c^3+4c^2-3c=0\Rightarrow c(2c-1)(2c+3)=0\). So \(\cos\theta=0\) (\(\theta=\frac\pi2,\frac{3\pi}2\)) or \(\cos\theta=\frac12\) (\(\theta=\frac\pi3,\frac{5\pi}3\)). Sum \(=2\pi+2\pi=4\pi\). Answer: (D).
authoredSolutions.56: The \(k\)-th term is \(\frac1k\cdot\frac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6}=\frac{(k+1)(2k+1)}{6}=\frac{2k^2+3k+1}{6}\). Summing to 10 terms: \(\frac16\big(2\sum k^2+3\sum k+\sum1\big)=\frac16(2\cdot385+3\cdot55+10)=\frac{945}{6}=\frac{315}{2}\). Answer: (C).
authoredSolutions.57: The lift skips floors 1 and 2 and reaches the 10th, so usable exit floors are 3 to 10, i.e. 8 floors. Choose the 4 persons who exit together: \(\binom94\). Assign a floor to the group of 4 and a different floor to the group of 5: \(8\times7\). Total \(=126\times56=7056\). Answer: (C).
authoredSolutions.58: Mean \(8\Rightarrow\alpha+\beta=56-40=16\). Variance \(16\Rightarrow\sum(x_i-8)^2=112\Rightarrow(\alpha-8)^2+(\beta-8)^2=8\). Writing \(\alpha=8-d,\ \beta=8+d\) gives \(2d^2=8\Rightarrow d=2\), so \(\alpha=6,\ \beta=10\). Roots are \(3\alpha+2=20\) and \(2\beta+1=21\); sum \(=41\), product \(=420\). Equation \(x^2-41x+420=0\). Answer: (B).
authoredSolutions.59: Total ways to split 12 balls into 6 unordered pairs: \(\frac{12!}{2^6\,6!}=10395\). Favourable (each pair one blue and one green) equals the number of matchings of 6 blue with 6 green, i.e. \(6!=720\). Probability \(=\frac{720}{10395}=\frac{16}{231}\). Answer: (C).
authoredSolutions.60: Touching the x-axis at \((3,0)\) gives centre \((3,k)\) with radius \(k\). The y-axis intercept \(2\sqrt{k^2-9}=6\sqrt3\Rightarrow k^2-9=27\Rightarrow k=6\). So centre \((3,6)\), \(r=6\). Distance to \(x-y-3=0\): \(\frac{|3-6-3|}{\sqrt2}=3\sqrt2\). Chord length \(=2\sqrt{36-18}=6\sqrt2\). Answer: (C).
authoredSolutions.61: For \(E\): \(\frac ae=\frac{4\sqrt6}{3}\Rightarrow a=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{4\sqrt6}{3}=2\sqrt2\) and \(b^2=a^2(1-e^2)=8\cdot\frac14=2\), so semi-major \(=2\sqrt2\) and minor axis \(=2\sqrt2\). For \(H\): \(e_H=2\sqrt2\Rightarrow\frac{b_H^2}{a_H^2}=e_H^2-1=7\); latus rectum \(\frac{2b_H^2}{a_H}=2\sqrt2\Rightarrow\frac{b_H^2}{a_H}=\sqrt2\Rightarrow 7a_H=\sqrt2\Rightarrow a_H=\frac{\sqrt2}{7}\). Distance between foci \(=2a_He_H=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{7}\cdot2\sqrt2=\frac87\). Answer: (D).
authoredSolutions.62: Directrix \(\frac ae=9\) with \(e=\frac13\Rightarrow a=3\), \(b^2=9(1-\frac19)=8\), focus \(P(ae,0)=(1,0)\). A midpoint \((h,k)\) satisfies \(T=S_1\): \(\frac{xh}{9}+\frac{yk}{8}=\frac{h^2}{9}+\frac{k^2}{8}\). Substituting \((1,0)\): \(\frac h9=\frac{h^2}{9}+\frac{k^2}{8}\). Multiplying by 72: \(9k^2=8h-8h^2=8h(1-h)\). Locus: \(9y^2=8x(1-x)\). Answer: (A).
authoredSolutions.63: Let \(\tan^{-1}(x\sqrt2)=A\Rightarrow\sin A=\frac{x\sqrt2}{\sqrt{1+2x^2}}\). Let \(\sin^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^2}=B\Rightarrow\cos B=x,\ \cot B=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\). Equating: \(\frac{x\sqrt2}{\sqrt{1+2x^2}}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\Rightarrow 2(1-x^2)=1+2x^2\Rightarrow x^2=\frac14\Rightarrow x=\frac12\). Answer: (A).
authoredSolutions.64: Directions \(\vec d_1=(1,2,-3),\ \vec d_2=(2,4,-5)\); \(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=(2,-1,0)\), \(|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|=\sqrt5\). authoredSolutions.65: \(2\vec a+3\vec b=(22,15,15)\) and \(\vec a-\vec b=(-4,0,0)\). Their cross product is \((0,-60,60)\) with magnitude \(60\sqrt2\). Triangle area \(=\frac12(60\sqrt2)=30\sqrt2\), so the square of the area is \(1800\). Answer: (C).
authoredSolutions.66: Since \(\tan(x-2)\sim(x-2)\), the limit reduces to \(\lim_{x\to2}\frac{rx^2+(p-2)x-2p}{x-2}=5\). The numerator must vanish at \(x=2\): \(4r-4=0\Rightarrow r=1\); it then factors as \((x-2)(x+p)\), so the limit is \(2+p=5\Rightarrow p=3\). For \(x^2-3x+q=0\) with both roots in \((0,2)\): \(f(0)=q>0\), \(f(2)=q-2>0\), discriminant \(9-4q\ge0\Rightarrow q\le\frac94\), vertex \(\frac32\in(0,2)\). So \(q\in(2,\frac94]\) and \(4(\alpha+\beta)=4(2+\frac94)=17\). Answer: (C).
authoredSolutions.67: Singular means \(\det A=3-\alpha=0\Rightarrow\alpha=3\). Here \(f(x)=\int_0^x(t^2+2t+3)\,dt=\frac{x^3}{3}+x^2+3x\) with \(f'(x)=x^2+2x+3>0\), so \(f\) increases on \([1,3]\). Thus \(M=f(3)=27\) and \(m=f(1)=\frac{13}{3}\), giving \(3(M-m)=3\cdot\frac{68}{3}=68\). Answer: (B).
authoredSolutions.68: Putting \(x=0\) in \(f(xy)=f(x)f(y)\) gives \(f(0)=f(0)f(y)\); since \(f(0)\neq0\), \(f\equiv1\). Then \(x^2g(x)=\int_1^x(t^2-tg(t))\,dt\). Differentiating: \(2xg+x^2g'=x^2-xg\Rightarrow g'+\frac3x g=1\). Integrating factor \(x^3\) gives \(x^3g=\frac{x^4}{4}+C\); \(g(1)=0\Rightarrow C=-\frac14\). So \(g(x)=\frac x4-\frac1{4x^3}\) and \(g(2)=\frac12-\frac1{32}=\frac{15}{32}\). Answer: (C).
authoredSolutions.69: The curves meet where \(x^2-8x=-x\Rightarrow x^2-7x=0\Rightarrow x=0,7\). Area \(=\int_0^7\big[-x-(x^2-8x)\big]\,dx=\int_0^7(7x-x^2)\,dx=\Big[\frac{7x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{3}\Big]_0^7=\frac{343}{2}-\frac{343}{3}=\frac{343}{6}\). Answer: (A).
authoredSolutions.70: The term \(\frac{x^3}{x^2+2|x|+1}\) is odd, so its integral over \([-1,1]\) is \(0\). The remaining part is even: \(\int_{-1}^1\frac{|x|+1}{(|x|+1)^2}\,dx=2\int_0^1\frac{x+1}{(x+1)^2}\,dx=2\int_0^1\frac{dx}{x+1}=2\log_e 2\). Answer: (B).
authoredSolutions.71: \(\log_e(x+y)\le2\Rightarrow x+y\le e^2\Rightarrow x+y\le7\) with \(x,y\in\mathbb{N}\). The element \(1\) is a hub: \((a,1)\) and \((1,c)\in R\) for all \(a,c\le6\), so the transitive closure contains all of \(\{1,\dots,6\}\times\{1,\dots,6\}\), i.e. \(36\) pairs. authoredSolutions.73: \(PQ=PR\) forces \(P\) onto the diameter through centre \((4,-3)\) perpendicular to \(x-y=4\). authoredSolutions.75: The function \(g\) has a jump only at input \(0\): the left value \((0-8)^{1/3}=-2\) and the right value \((0+4)^{1/2}=2\). Now \(f\) itself jumps at \(x=0\) (from \(8\) to \(-4\)), giving one discontinuity of \(g\circ f\). Also \(f(x)=0\) at \(x=-2\) and \(x=2\), where \(f\) crosses \(0\); there \(g\circ f\) jumps from \(-2\) to \(2\). Hence \(g\circ f\) is discontinuous at \(x=-2,0,2\), i.e. \(3\) points. Answer: 3.
